They help reduce costs while improving scalability and fidelity. However, their successful implementation is context-dependent, and existing research offers limited guidance on how the implementation of digital parenting interventions unfolds across diverse settings. Objective: This study aims to identify the shared and unique facilitators and barriers affecting each dimension of imple- mentation, as well as differentiated mechanisms that support the effective implementation and institutionalization of such interventions across diverse settings. Methods: Using a multiple-case study design, this research compared the implementation of a digital (chatbot-led) parenting program across 2 distinct settings in China: urban educational and rural health care contexts. The intervention content remained consistent, while the contexts and formats of local human-led support differed. Guided by the RE-AIM framework, this study examines the program’s reach, adoption, implementation, and maintenance in both settings. Data sources included program documents, field observations, semistructured interviews, and focus group discussions with 83 stakeholders. Thematic analysis was conducted using ATLAS.ti until thematic saturation was reached. Results: Data were collected from 83 stakeholders, and findings are based on an analysis of 18 interviews and 4 focus groups with caregivers, village doctors, and health officials from the rural health care setting, and 29 interviews and 4 focus groups with caregivers, teachers, social workers, and managers from the urban educational setting. Regarding reach, strong relationships between parents and implementers and the credibility of program developers were shared facilitators in both settings. Parenting conservatism and limited understanding of the program were shared barriers. In rural health care settings, parents’ perception of village doctors as lacking parenting expertise posed an additional challenge. For adoption, trust between managers and program developers, program alignment with organizational functions, and organizational empower- ment supported implementation are shared facilitators in both settings. At the individual level, task-driven motivation helped, https://www.jmir.org/2026/1/e79848 J Med Internet Res 2026 | vol. 28 | e79848 | p. 1 (page number not for citation purposes) JOURNAL OF MEDICAL INTERNET RESEARCH Shi et al while time constraints hindered adoption in the health care setting. Teachers adopted the program due to its relevance to their roles in the educational setting, unlike village doctors, who did not see it as part of their core duties. For implemen- tation, supportive management and clear guidelines were shared facilitators in both settings, while a lack of purpose and psychological pressure acted as barriers. Rural implementation was aided by scheduling during off-seasons and standardized workflows, whereas flexible workflows were essential in the educational setting. Regarding maintenance, alignment with organizational functions and internal resources facilitated sustainability in both settings, while overreliance on government authorization posed challenges. Educational settings required contextual adaptation, while health care settings needed more content adaptation. Conclusions: Implementing digital parenting programs is a complex process, influenced by multilevel facilitators and barriers that vary across regions (rural vs urban) and settings (educational vs health care). This study highlights the importance of context-specific implementation strategies and proposes differentiated delivery models tailored to local structures and needs. JSON: Name: digital_parenting_reaim_pipeline Title: Comparative RE-AIM multiple-case implementation study of hybrid digital parenting interventions to improve institutionalization in low-resource health-care and educational settings in China Short Hypothesis: Embedding a culturally adapted chatbot-based parenting program within trusted local human-led channels (teachers in urban preschools; village doctors in rural health centers) increases reach, staff adoption, implementation fidelity, and 12-month maintenance compared with chatbot-only delivery in low-resource Chinese settings. Related Work: Existing work demonstrates that digital parenting interventions can improve parental knowledge and child outcomes and that adding human-led support generally increases engagement and efficacy. Prior implementation studies have used frameworks such as RE-AIM to evaluate digital health programs in high-resource settings, and process evaluations in LMICs have documented context-specific barriers to scale-up. Limitations of current approaches include: predominance of efficacy evidence from high-income countries, limited comparative analyses across distinct service systems (education vs health care), sparse quantitative measurement of institutionalization and maintenance, inadequate guidance on incentive structures for frontline implementers, and few mixed-methods pipelines linking RE-AIM metrics to pragmatic adaptations for scale in low-resource contexts. Abstract: Problem: Institutionalizing evidence-based digital parenting programs in low-resource settings requires context-specific implementation strategies, but comparative evidence across service sectors is scarce. Approach: We propose a mixed-methods research pipeline combining (1) multiple-case qualitative RE-AIM analyses in urban preschool and rural health-center settings to map facilitators and barriers, and (2) a cluster-randomized pragmatic trial comparing chatbot-only delivery versus hybrid chatbot-plus-local-human-support models (teacher-led group support in preschools; village-doctor home visits in rural clinics). Contribution: The pipeline quantifies RE-AIM outcomes (reach, adoption, fidelity, maintenance), links them to organizational and staff-level mechanisms, and evaluates cost and sustainment at 6 and 12 months. Expected outcome: Evidence-based, sector-specific implementation models and decision rules for hybrid digital parenting delivery that optimize institutional adoption and long-term maintenance in low-resource regions. Experiments: Design: Multi-site, cluster-randomized pragmatic trial with mixed-method process evaluation informed by prior multiple-case RE-AIM analysis. Sites and datasets: 1) Pilot qualitative dataset from two earlier cases (urban preschool, two rural townships); 2) Cluster RCT across N_preschools = 60 preschools and N_health_centers = 60 township health centers stratified by region (total 120 clusters). Each cluster recruits ~25 eligible primary caregivers (total participants ≈ 3000). Arms: A) chatbot-only (digital content via WeChat chatbot), B) chatbot + human support (in preschools: teacher-facilitated WeChat group + optional parent meetings; in health centers: village-doctor biweekly home visits + phone follow-ups), C) usual care (if ethically feasible) or delayed-start control. Baselines: chatbot-only and usual care. Metrics (primary implementation endpoints): Reach = % eligible caregivers enrolling and activating chatbot; Adoption = % clusters and frontline staff initiating delivery; Implementation fidelity = standardized checklist score (0-100) measured by independent auditors; Maintenance = proportion of clusters delivering program at 6 and 12 months post-trial start. Secondary outcomes: caregiver engagement (modules completed, time spent), parenting practice change (validated self-report scales), child development (ASQ-3 or equivalent age-appropriate instrument), incremental cost per engaged family. Evaluation: generalized linear mixed models (GLMM) for binary outcomes and linear mixed models for continuous outcomes with random intercepts for cluster and site, covariate adjustment (baseline demographics), multiple comparisons corrected via Benjamini-Hochberg; mediation analysis to test whether fidelity mediates the effect of human support on maintenance; subgroup analyses for left-behind children, migrant-parent households, and staff workload level. Ablations: compare group-based vs individual human support (within hybrid arm strata) and incentive type (material stipend vs recognition/certificate) using factorial nested design in a subset of clusters. Power: design powered to detect a 10 percentage-point absolute increase in adoption (α=0.05, 80% power) assuming ICC=0.05; final sample size to be verified by formal power calculations. Data collection timeline: baseline, 3 months (reach/adoption/fidelity), 6 months (implementation outcomes; interim maintenance), 12 months (maintenance, child outcomes). Qualitative component: longitudinal semi-structured interviews and FGDs with managers, implementers, and caregivers sampled purposively across arms for thematic analysis mapped to RE-AIM. Risk Factors and Limitations: Technical and logistical: inconsistent mobile connectivity, platform downtime, or changes to the hosting environment could reduce digital reach and bias comparisons; seasonal migration and farming cycles may confound reach and maintenance in rural sites. Measurement and bias: self-reported parenting outcomes are susceptible to social desirability and recall bias; fidelity audits may be subject to observer effects. Cluster and contamination risks: cross-cluster information sharing could dilute arm contrasts; staff turnover may alter adoption and fidelity. Generalizability and sample bias: results from selected provinces and partnered organizations may not generalize to other regions or countries with different service structures or cultural norms. Resource and scalability constraints: hybrid human support models require sustained incentives and supervisory capacity; if cost per engaged family is high, maintenance will be limited. Ethical and equity concerns: differential access for caregivers without smartphones or with low literacy may systematically exclude vulnerable subgroups. Analytical limitations: unmeasured confounders at cluster level and imperfect ICC estimates could reduce power; mediation analyses may be limited by temporal resolution and causality assumptions.
